newsitem.title: UK: Forecasters see no relief for drought-hit crops.
newsitem.headline: Forecasters see no relief for drought-hit crops.

text.p: After an unusually dry winter and early spring in Britain and France weather forecasters cannot hold out any promise of rain for a grain trade getting increasingly jumpy about the possible effects of drought on crops.
Climatologists do not know the cause of the persisent dry weather. The change in weather patterns is more than they had expected from global warming.
Forecasters expect dry weather to continue for now.
But in most cases their analysis does not go beyond the end of the month. "It's a bit too far ahead for the computer models," said Jim Hales of Birmingham University's Geography department.

Hales, a climatologist, said the prevalence of high pressure was responsible for the dry weather. "Basically it's a question of pressure. The air aloft is stable and you're unlikely to get any substantial rainfall," he said.

High pressure over central and southern Europe and Spain had kept rain-bearing fronts away from Britain. The south and east of England have been worst hit. Scotland and Northern Ireland have had more rain, he said.
Farming sector analysts hope that the dry weather does not go on for too long.
"It would be very surprising if we don't get some significant rain in April," one farming analyst said. "But there's cause for concern."
But weather forecasters hold out little hope. "There's no sign of rain at the moment for the next two months," a spokesman for the Meteorological Office said.
The past 24 months have been the driest since March 1749 to 1751, the spokesman said.
"And it's been a very dry start to the year," he said. Rainfall in January was just 18 percent of the average. February was above average at 139 percent but March was 32 percent.

Birmingham's Hales put river levels at 35 percent of normal in the Severn and low in the Derwent and Thames. He had measured just 3 millimetres of rain in Birmingham since the beginning of April. "The lack of rain is quite staggering," he said.

Not only do the climate experts not know what has caused the long dry spell -- the size of the apparent shift in patterns also puzzles them. "It is large, larger than in the models, which means it cannot entirely be blamed on man-made effects," said Geoff Jenkins of the Hadley Centre for Climate Prediction and Research.
On Tuesday French authorities in provinces around Paris ordered farmers to suspend irrigation for 48 hours each weekend, and British farmers in East Anglia face restrictions on water usage.
"It's probable, rather than possible, that restrictions will be widespread," a spokesman for the Environment Agency said.
The last two years have been the driest on record for the major grain-growing region and groundwater levels are precariously low.

Even without irrigation restrictions, some farmers will struggle to make up for stress already affecting autumn-sown crops, a French farm ministry source said. --Christopher Lyddon, London newsroom +44 171 542 7928
